rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tibaq primarily means conforming with one another; Asad directs readers to 2:20 for the meaning of the seven heavens.
rows.anchor: this being the primary significance of tibaq (sing. tabaq). For the meaning of the "seven heavens", see surah 2, note 20.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the earth submissive means that it yields to the intelligence God has endowed in human beings.
rows.anchor: Lit., "who has made the earth submissive (dhalulan) to you": i.e., yielding to the intelligence with which He has endowed man.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walking prone symbolizes spiritual obtuseness: a person sees only immediate worldly concerns and has no sense of the direction of the path, like an earthworm.
rows.anchor: seeing only what is immediately beneath his feet, and utterly unaware of the direction into which his path is taking him

rows.speaker: author
rows.anchor: Lit., "We shall brand him on the snout" (khurtum).

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: Commentators read the snout-branding idiom as indelible disgrace; Asad cites Lane quoting Raghib and Taj al-'Arus.
rows.anchor: All commentators point out that this, idiomatic phrase has a strictly metaphorical meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means an inquirer inquired, though Asad also allows the rendering might inquire.
rows.anchor: Lit.," An inquirer inquired" or "might inquire".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders ruh as inspiration and refers readers to his note on 16:2.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of ruh as "inspiration", see surah 16, note 2.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi understands the angels' and inspiration's ascent as the return of all things to God as their source.
rows.anchor: The "ascent" of the angels and of all inspiration may be understood in the same sense as the frequently-occurring phrase "all things go back to God [as their source]" (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is timeless, so a day, aeon, thousand years, or fifty thousand years are alike to Him and have apparent reality only in creation; Asad connects this with 22:47.
rows.anchor: a day, or an aeon, or a thousand years, or fifty thousand years are alike to Him, having an apparent reality only within the created world and none with the Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since time will also cease to mean anything to people in the hereafter, asking when the wicked will be punished and the righteous rewarded is irrelevant.
rows.anchor: in the hereafter time will cease to have a meaning for man as well, it is irrelevant to ask as to "when" the evildoers will be chastised and the righteous given their due

rows.speaker: Abu Muslim
rows.claim: Abu Muslim, as quoted by Razi, takes abundant water as a metaphor for happiness that echoes the Qur'an's allegorical running waters of paradise.
rows.anchor: a metaphor of happiness, echoing the allegorical reference, so frequently occurring in the Qur'an, to the "running waters" of paradise (Abu Muslim, quoted by Razi)

rows.speaker: Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Al-Hasan
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Al-Hasan explain ar-ruh here as the plural human souls, although the Arabic says "the soul" in the singular.
rows.anchor: according to Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Al~Hasan (all of them quoted by Tabari), the meaning of ar-ruh in the above context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement includes the prophets' symbolic right to intercede, but such intercession requires God's leave and implies His prior acceptance of the sinner's repentance, as 10:3 and note 7 explain.
rows.anchor: This includes the symbolic right of the prophets to "intercede" for the sinners on Judgment Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, anyone God permits to speak on Judgment Day will say only what is right, making untruthfulness impossible.
rows.anchor: the impossibility of anyone's being untruthful on Judgment Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's claim to divine status is his cardinal sin and the transgression of right; Asad cross-references 28:38 and its note 36.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh's claim to divine status is the cardinal sin whereby "he has transgressed all bounds of what is right" (verse 17 above).

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad reports that some authorities date the surah to early Mecca, while others consider it more likely to belong to the last group of Meccan revelations.
rows.anchor: others regard it as more probable that it belongs to the last group of Meccan revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders thumma at the start as "And once again" and refers to 6:31.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of thumma at the beginning of this verse as "And once again", see surah 6, note 31.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the question stresses that human intellect and imagination cannot grasp Judgment Day, a reality beyond experience; allegory and emotional response only offer an inkling.
rows.anchor: man's intellect and imagination cannot possibly answer it, since what is described as the Day of Judgment will usher in a reality which as yet is wholly outside our human experience
